problems.stem: A department lead announces: 'We picked the new LMS analytics dashboard; now let's figure out what problems it solves.' Why does this sequence violate the principle of naming design tensions before tool choice?
options: Analytics dashboards are never appropriate in classrooms.
The tool was selected before the competing classroom values it must trade off were even surfaced, so the choice cannot be defended as a resolution of any tension.
The department should have asked the vendor first.
Dashboards must always be chosen by a committee.
problems.explanation: Naming tensions first means surfacing the competing values (for example, monitoring versus student autonomy) before adoption, so the tool is chosen to resolve a known tension rather than to manufacture one.

problems.stem: A teacher names the tension as 'fast feedback vs. teacher workload.' A colleague says this is not yet a design tension a tool choice can resolve. What is the most accurate critique?
options: Both sides of a design tension should serve student interests; 'teacher workload' is a constraint, but the real value conflict is between fast feedback and the depth or fairness of that feedback.
Feedback speed does not matter in any classroom.
Tensions can only have one side, not two.
Teacher workload should never be considered.
problems.explanation: A genuine design tension pits two values that both have legitimate claims on the learning. Workload is a real constraint, but framing the tension around competing learning values (speed vs. depth/fairness) is what a tool choice can actually be tested against.

problems.stem: Before choosing a tool, a teacher asks an AI to 'recommend the best app for differentiated reading.' The AI names one. What is the defensible way to use this output given the section's principle?
options: Adopt the recommended app, since differentiation is a recognized goal.
First use the AI to help enumerate the competing values at stake (for example, personalization vs. shared class discussion), then evaluate any tool against that named tension.
Ask the AI to also write the lesson plan and grade it.
Ignore the AI entirely because tool recommendations are off-limits.
problems.explanation: A tool recommendation skips the step that matters: surfacing the tension. AI is most defensibly used to help name competing values, after which any candidate tool is judged against that tension.

problems.stem: A teacher claims to have resolved the tension between 'monitoring engagement' and 'student privacy' by buying a camera-based attention tracker, saying 'the tension is gone now.' Why is this resolution not yet defensible?
options: Cameras are always banned in schools.
A defensible resolution shows how the chosen tool negotiates BOTH values and what was given up; declaring the tension gone hides the privacy cost that was actually paid.
Engagement cannot be monitored at all.
The teacher should have bought two trackers.
problems.explanation: Resolving a tension is not eliminating one side. A defensible decision shows the negotiated position, what each value gained, and what was traded away. Claiming the tension is 'gone' conceals the privacy cost.
